title: Grateful Dead Live at Hollywood Palladium on 1971-08-06
lineage: SHN -> Cool Edit Pro v2.0 -> Samplitude Professional v9.12 -> FLAC
source: (FOB) Sony ECM-22P -> Master Reel -> Reel -> Dat -> Cool Edit Pro -> SHN D

ai_review.summary: An outstanding audience recording that captures a high‑energy 1971 show highlighted by a monster “Hard to Handle” and superb renditions of Lovelight, Me & Bobby McGee, and the Other One sequence.
ai_review.review: This Charlie Miller‑mastered audience tape is praised as one of the best AUDs ever released, with clear enough sound that drums, bass and vocals are all discernible despite a slight tinny quality on the kit. The performance itself is described as tight, upbeat and “smokin”, featuring a legendary Hard to Handle, an epic Lovelight, and several other classic ’71 moments like Brokedown Palace and Me & Bobby McGee.

ai_rating.rationale: Over 40 reviews, virtually all 5‑star, repeatedly cite both stellar musical performance and exceptional audience recording quality; only minor technical quibbles are noted.

recording_quality.technical_notes: Despite being an audience source the tape is remarkably clear; drums are a bit tinny, bass slightly muddy and vocals a touch low, but overall balance is superb for a 1971 AUD thanks to Charlie Miller’s mastering.

standout_songs: The Other One > Me & My Uncle > The Other One
show_quality.setlist_flow: The set is described as tight, well‑rehearsed and upbeat with a second set that “rocks”; transitions flow naturally and the band feeds off an enthusiastic crowd.

band_member_comments.Jerry: Multiple reviewers note his soaring solo on Hard to Handle (some say he even dropped to his knees) and praise his clean, soulful tone throughout the show.
band_member_comments.Phil: His playing is credited with energizing the crowd; one reviewer mentions Phil “bombs” and that the audience’s frenzy was partly due to his bass work.
band_member_comments.Bob: Bob Weir’s interaction (telling the taper to move back 40 ft) and his vocal performance are highlighted as among his best, adding humor and warmth to the show.
band_member_comments.Drums: Even without Mickey Hart the drumming is described as hard‑driving, powerful and “tinny” only in a technical sense; the rhythm section propels the high‑energy set.
